hints: Start from the outside world - what does the nervous system need to pick up first before it can coordinate any response?
Think about the form of energy in a stimulus, such as light or pressure, compared with the form of energy in a nerve impulse - what type of conversion must the receptor cell carry out?
Think about what electrical change is first produced in the receptor and where that signal must be passed next to reach the CNS.
walkthrough:
Detecting a Change in the Environment**
Sensory receptor cells sit at the start of the pathway. They detect a specific stimulus such as light, sound, touch, pressure, pain, chemicals, heat or tension. Without them the nervous system would have no information about changes inside or outside the body.

Transducing Energy into Electricity**
A stimulus is a form of energy, but neurones communicate electrically. The receptor acts as a transducer, converting stimulus energy into electrical energy. This produces a small depolarisation called a generator or receptor potential.

Starting the Sensory Pathway**
If that generator potential is large enough it will trigger an action potential that is then passed on to and along a sensory neurone toward the central nervous system for processing.

Final answer: Detect / respond to changes in stimuli, e.g. light and sound; act as transducers converting stimulus energy into electrical energy to produce a generator / receptor potential; pass impulse to / along a sensory neurone.

hints: Remind yourself of the shape of an action potential - which part of Fig. 8.1 is rising steeply, which is falling, and which is flat at resting potential?
Link rising membrane potential to entry of positive ions and falling membrane potential to exit of positive ions - which voltage-gated channels must be open in each phase?
Remember the $Na^+/K^+$ pump restores ion gradients using ATP after and during repolarisation - at which letters is the membrane returning to and maintaining the resting potential near $-70$ $mV$?
walkthrough:
Reading Phase C - Rapid Depolarisation**
At C the trace rises sharply from about $-50$ $mV$ through $0$ $mV$ toward $+40$ $mV$. This is depolarisation caused by voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels opening and $Na^+$ flooding into the axon down its electrochemical gradient.

Reading Phase D - Rapid Repolarisation**
At D the trace falls sharply from $+40$ $mV$ back down. Here voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels have closed and voltage-gated $K^+$ channels are open, so $K^+$ leaves the axon and the inside becomes negative again.

Pump Activity to Restore Gradients**
The $Na^+/K^+$ pump uses ATP to move $3Na^+$ out and $2K^+$ in to re-establish the resting ion distributions. It contributes during repolarisation at D and in maintaining the resting potential at E around $-70$ $mV$.
Final answer: $Na^+/K^+$ pump is operating: D and E (C also operating); voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels are open: C; voltage-gated $K^+$ channels are open: D.

hints: Compare the size of the small bump after stimulus A with the dashed threshold line at about $-50$ $mV$ - did A reach that line?
Recall what must happen to voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels for a full action potential to fire - what name is given to the small depolarisation that fails to do this?
walkthrough:
Sub-threshold Versus Supra-threshold**
After A the membrane depolarises slightly from $-70$ $mV$ to about $-60$ $mV$ but stays well below the dashed threshold potential at about $-50$ $mV$. This is just a generator potential. After B the membrane rapidly crosses threshold.

All-or-Nothing Firing**
Only when threshold is reached do enough voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels open to cause the positive feedback of depolarisation to $+40$ $mV$. Because A was too weak in intensity, threshold was not crossed and no action potential was produced.

Final answer: Stimulus A produced only a small generator / receptor potential; threshold potential (about $-50$ $mV$) was not reached / exceeded, so voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels did not open fully and no action potential fired, whereas stimulus B depolarised beyond threshold.

hints: Think about what the membrane cannot do immediately after an action potential while $Na^+$ channels are inactivated and $K^+$ channels are still open.
Think about why it is useful that the region just behind a moving impulse cannot fire again straight away - what does this ensure about direction and separation of signals?
walkthrough:
Recovery Time Limits Frequency**
During the refractory period voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels are closed and inactivated, so a new action potential cannot start immediately. This sets a minimum time between impulses and therefore a maximum frequency, keeping impulses as separate signals.

Enforcing One-Way Flow**
Because the patch of membrane just behind the advancing impulse is refractory, only the patch ahead can be depolarised to threshold. The impulse therefore cannot turn back and must move forward in one direction toward the synapse.

Final answer: Limits / controls maximum frequency of action potentials so impulses remain separate; ensures action potentials / impulses travel in one direction only, as the region just behind cannot be re-stimulated.

hints: Start with what an action potential creates - a region of positive charge inside - and how that charge can affect the resting region next to it.
Remember myelin made by Schwann cells is an electrical insulator impermeable to ions - where are the only gaps where ions can move?
Think about what happens when the local current reaches the next gap - which channels open and what is regenerated there?
Put the speed and direction together - what name is given to this jumping mode and why is it one-way?
walkthrough:
Local Circuits Ahead of the Impulse**
An action potential leaves the inside of the membrane positively charged compared with the resting region ahead. $Na^+$ and other positive ions are attracted sideways, setting up a local circuit that depolarises the next region toward threshold.

Myelin Forces Jumping Between Nodes**
In a myelinated axon the Schwann cells and myelin sheath insulate the axon and are impermeable to $Na^+$ and $K^+$, so ion movement and depolarisation cannot occur under the myelin. The only exposed membrane is at nodes of Ranvier where voltage-gated channels are concentrated.

Regeneration at the Next Node**
When the local current reaches the next node it opens voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels there, triggering a fresh action potential. The signal therefore appears to jump from node to node.

Saltatory Conduction**
This is saltatory conduction. Because each node fires only after the previous one and the previous region is refractory, transmission is one-way and much faster than in an unmyelinated axon, as fewer action potentials need to be generated.

Final answer: Depolarised region sets up local circuits with ions moving from positive to negative region ahead; myelin sheath insulates axon preventing ion movement except at nodes of Ranvier; depolarisation opens voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels at next node causing new action potential / depolarisation; action potentials jump node to node by saltatory conduction in one direction, which is faster.
